title: Project: design an AI helper
essentialQuestion: How would you design an AI helper that is useful, fair and safe?
learningGoal: Plan a helper for a problem many people share: say who it helps, whether AI fits, how to check that it works, and how to improve it after feedback.

warmUp.question: Which of these jobs could an AI helper do well?
options: Sorting rubbish into the right bin
Guessing when a bus will come

evidence.question: For each project, what problem does it start from, what does the AI do, and what do people still do? What evidence is there that it works?

cards.title: Two real projects in Southeast Asia

cases.name: Eco Pulse, Malaysia: a student prototype
cases.body: The problem: the students wanted to make recycling quicker and easier for the people who do it. Who built it: three 15-year-old students at SMK Sultan Ismail, a secondary school in Johor. What the AI does: an app looks at a photo of a recyclable item and estimates its weight and value. The evidence: it won an award in a 2024 student competition run by Samsung in Malaysia. The organiser says it is precise, but no test results have been published. A question: how well does it work with dirty or crushed items?

cases.name: Traffy Fondue, Thailand: a public service in use
cases.body: The problem: residents see broken roads, floods and broken street lights, and need the right office to fix them. Who built and uses it: a national science agency built it. Residents send a report with a photo and a place, and city and local offices answer. What the AI does: it sorts each report by type and sends it to the right office. People there decide what to do and do the repairs. The evidence: its makers say it received over 940,000 reports from 2022 to 2024. That shows it is used, not how well each problem was fixed. A question: how can people without a smartphone or the internet report a problem?

activity.title: Plan your AI helper
activity.instructions: Plan a helper in five steps. Pick one of the made-up Maple Street problems, or a problem that many people share in a community you know. Don't write anyone's real name or private information. You can go back and change any step.

problems.text: Maple Street (made up): plastic often goes in the wrong bin at the centre.
Maple Street (made up): the bus is often late, and people wait in the rain.
Maple Street (made up): the garden tap at the centre is often left running.
A problem many people share in a community I know

steps.title: 1. The problem
steps.prompt: What is the problem, and who does it affect? How would a helper make things better for them?

steps.title: 2. Should AI be used?
steps.prompt: Think about three questions. Does the helper need to recognise or guess from many examples? Could a simple rule or a person do it better? Could it hurt someone if it is wrong? Then decide.

options.feedback: Go on to step 3. In your plan, say why AI fits: what must it recognise or guess?
That is a good design choice too. Write the other way, and why it fits better, like the club's buddy group.
That is fine. Write what you still need to find out, and decide again after step 4.

steps.title: 3. What it learns from
steps.prompt: What examples would it learn from? Who would label them? Whose examples might be missing? If you chose another way, say what it needs instead.
steps.starter: It would learn from ... Examples of ___ might be missing.

steps.title: 4. Risks, tests and checks
steps.prompt: What could go wrong? How would you test that it works? Who would check it, and how often?
steps.starter: One risk is ... To test it, ... ___ would check it by ...

steps.title: 5. Feedback and version 2
steps.prompt: Read your plan to a partner, or read it again yourself. Answer one of these questions. Then change one thing.
questions: Who might this helper leave out?
What happens if it makes a mistake?
Is there a simpler way without AI?
What evidence would show that it helps?

activity.saves: The learner's choices and short answers, with the lesson's other writing, on this device only. While “just looking around”, nothing is saved.
activity.offline: Everything is in the lesson file. Nothing is built, run or sent anywhere.

sections.heading: Start with the problem, not the tool
sections.text: In this project, you will plan a helper for a problem that many people share in a community. Good designers start with the problem and the people it affects, not the tool. In Malaysia, three 15-year-old students wanted to make recycling easier, so they built a prototype app, Eco Pulse, that estimates the weight and value of items from a photo. Then designers ask: should AI be used here at all? AI can help when a helper must recognise or guess from many examples. But sometimes a simple rule or a person does the job better. The made-up Maple Street design club decided a tool should not choose friends, because people should choose their own.
sections.simpler: You will plan a helper for a shared problem. Good designers start with the problem and the people it affects. In Malaysia, three 15-year-old students wanted easier recycling. They built a prototype app, Eco Pulse. From a photo of rubbish, it tries to tell the weight and value. Should AI be used here? AI can help when a helper must learn from many examples. Sometimes a simple rule or a person is better. The made-up Maple Street club said no to a tool that chooses friends. People should choose their own.

sections.heading: Plan what it learns and what could go wrong
sections.text: Next, a designer plans what the helper will learn from. The club's bin helper would learn from photos of rubbish that club members label “plastic” or “paper”. These labelled examples are its training data. As you learned in Lesson 8, a tool can fail for anything missing from its examples, so the club adds photos of crushed and dirty items too. Then the designer lists the risks: a camera near the bins must never film people's faces. Finally, the designer decides who checks the helper. The club will look inside the bins every Friday.
sections.simpler: The bin helper learns from photos of rubbish that club members label. These are its training data. A tool can fail when examples are missing. So the club adds crushed rubbish too. One risk: the camera must never film faces. Last, decide who checks it: the club looks in the bins every Friday.

sections.heading: Test, listen and improve
sections.text: Designers also ask what evidence shows that a helper works. Eco Pulse won a student award, but no test results have been published yet. In Thailand, Traffy Fondue's AI sorts residents' reports about problems such as floods and sends each to the right office, where people fix them. Its makers count over 940,000 reports, but a count shows use, not how well problems were fixed. Designers test their plan with users, listen to feedback, change it and test again. This is called iteration. When the club's bus-timing helper went wrong after new roadworks, they added new examples. Share your plan, change one thing, and you have version 2.
sections.simpler: What shows that it works? Eco Pulse won an award, but no test results are published yet. In Thailand, Traffy Fondue's AI sorts reports about problems like floods. It sends each to the right office, where people fix them. Its makers count over 940,000 reports. That shows use, not how well problems were fixed. Designers test with users, listen to feedback and change the plan. This is called iteration. Change one thing for version 2.

glossary.definition: A person who plans how something will look and work.
glossary.example: The Maple Street club are designers. They plan helpers.

glossary.definition: A first test version of something, made to try out an idea.
glossary.example: Eco Pulse is a prototype. It still needs testing.

glossary.definition: Examples used to build an AI tool, like labelled photos.
glossary.example: The bin helper's training data is labelled photos of rubbish.

glossary.definition: The chance that something bad could happen.
glossary.example: One risk is that the camera films people's faces.

glossary.definition: What other people tell you about your work, to help you improve it.
glossary.example: A partner's feedback helped the club change its plan.

glossary.definition: Testing a plan, changing it, and testing it again, many times.
glossary.example: After the roadworks, iteration made the bus helper better.

checks.question: Why did the club drop the friend chooser?

options.text: The camera at the centre was broken that day
options.feedback: Not quite. The friend chooser had no camera. Read the first section.

options.text: People should choose their own friends
options.feedback: Yes. Some choices belong to people. The club planned a buddy group run by people instead.

options.text: Computers are too slow to choose friends
options.feedback: Not quite. Speed was not the reason. Read the first section about when AI should not be used.

checks.question: What does the evidence show about Eco Pulse so far?

options.text: It is a prototype that won an award
options.feedback: Yes. An award is a good start. It is not proof that the app works well for everyone.

options.text: It works well everywhere in Malaysia
options.feedback: Not quite. It is a student prototype, and no test results are published yet. Read the third section.

options.text: It was never built or tried
options.feedback: Not quite. The students built a prototype app. Read the first section.

checks.question: What problem that many people share could a helper help with? You can pick one from the lesson.

write.prompt: Write your plan for a helper. Say the problem and who it helps, whether AI fits or what you still need to find out, how you would check it works, and one change after feedback.
sentenceStarters: A helper would make things better by ...
I think AI fits / another way fits / I still need to find out ..., because ...
selfCheck: I said the problem, who it affects and how a helper would help.
I said if AI fits, or what I still need to find out, and why.
I said how to check it works, and one change after feedback.
write.example: The problem is that plastic often goes in the paper bin at the centre. It affects the people who sort the bins by hand. A helper would make sorting faster. I think AI fits, because it must recognise many kinds of rubbish from photos. It would learn from photos we label “plastic” or “paper”. To check it works, the club would test it on new photos and look in the bins every Friday. After feedback, I changed my plan to add photos of crushed bottles.

speak.partnerTask: Explain your plan to a partner in one minute: the problem, who it helps, and why AI fits or not. Your partner asks one question from step 5. Change one thing, and say your version 2.
speak.independentTask: Say your plan out loud. Then ask yourself who it might leave out and how you would know it works, and answer.

watch.title: What is AI?
watch.why: This short cartoon goes over training data, and why people must use AI with care.
watch.beforeQuestion: What do you remember about how AI learns?
watch.afterQuestion: Why do people need to be careful when they make or use AI?
watch.summary: This short cartoon goes over the basics of AI. AI tools learn from training data. This is a large set of examples that helps them find patterns and make guesses. Some AI tools sort things or make guesses about them. Other tools, called generative AI, make new things, like writing or pictures. The video explains that AI can be very useful, but it is not perfect. It learns from what people give it, so it can repeat their mistakes. That is why the people who make and use AI need to be responsible. They need to check its answers and think about who it might affect. This is a good review before you design your own AI helper.
keyPoints: AI learns patterns from training data.
Generative AI makes new things, like writing or pictures.
People who make and use AI must be responsible and check it.
watch.contentNote: An American cartoon for middle school, 2 minutes 37 seconds. It goes over ideas from Lessons 1 to 3 and mentions generative AI. The summary was written from Common Sense Education's description, not from watching it. Preview it first; learners can read the written summary instead.

sensitiveNotes: Problems must be ones that many people share in a community, not personal ones. Don't ask learners about problems in their own life, home or family. If a learner picks a problem about health, safety, legal matters or a particular person, gently steer them to one of the lesson's problems.
Plans are saved with the learner's work on this device. Learners must not write real people's names or private information in them.
educatorNotes: This is a design on paper: nothing is built, and coding is optional. Assess five things, not how impressive or how wary the plan sounds: the need (a real problem and who it affects), the intended benefit, technical fit (why AI helps, why another way fits better, or what the learner still needs to find out: all three are strong answers), evidence and checks (how they would test it, and who checks), and one improvement after feedback. It covers UNESCO's AI system design aspect at the Understand level and touches Create. Paper version: the five steps as a worksheet. Older or more confident learners can add a test plan (which new examples, and what result would count as working) or, optionally, build a tiny sorter with Lesson 3's nearest-neighbour idea.

The two real projects. Eco Pulse is known only from its organiser's account (Samsung Malaysia, 11 December 2024; also The Star, 26 January 2025): team TerraInnovators, three 15-year-olds at SMK Sultan Ismail, Johor, with an AI image-recognition app that estimates the weight and value of recyclable items, shown as a prototype at the Solve for Tomorrow 2024 final (run with Universiti Malaya). “With precision” is the organiser's claim; no test results are published, and it is not a working national service. Traffy Fondue (NECTEC, NSTDA) is an operating service: NSTDA reports over 940,000 reports from June 2022 to July 2024 and 77% “completed”, its own figures; a study of Bangkok's use (Hansen and Dahiya, 2025) notes it is digital-only, so people without smartphones or internet can be left out. Use each card's question for discussion, not as criticism of the people who built them.

Revised on 1 November 2026 from Justin's review: the evidence is now two real Southeast Asian projects, each with the problem and the people affected, who built or used it and what the AI does, what evidence exists, and one realistic question: Eco Pulse (Malaysia; three 15-year-old students; a prototype with an award, accuracy claimed but not published) and Traffy Fondue (Thailand; an operating public service where AI sorts and routes residents' reports and people do the repairs; report counts are not problems fixed). So the evidence is fictional: false, and the made-up Maple Street plans stay in the reading (labelled made up) and as the activity's starter problems (now marked “made up”). The design steps, Write task, starters, self-check, example and teacher notes now assess need, benefit, technical fit, evidence and checks, and improvement, and accept “AI helps”, “another way fits better” or “I still need to find out” with reasons; coding stays optional. Training data is defined as examples used to build a tool, not as always having the right answer; “prototype” added to the glossary. The second quick check now asks what the evidence shows about Eco Pulse. The Kyiv Polytechnic commentary was dropped from the sources to make room.
